questions.q: What is the main benefit of having a program read command line arguments?
choices: The program's behavior can change from run to run without modifying the code and recompiling it
The program compiles faster because fewer values are written into the source
The program no longer needs a main function
The program can only be run with one specific input file
questions.explain: Command line arguments specify input values or options at run time, so running with different arguments changes behavior without editing or recompiling the code.

questions.q: A program that takes an input filename as a command line argument can be run on any input file, unlike a program that names a specific input file in its code.
questions.explain: Passing the filename as an argument makes the program more general purpose: the user picks the file each time they run it.

questions.q: Which definition of main lets a C program receive command line arguments?
questions.explain: main must declare two parameters: argc (an int) first, then argv (an array of strings).

questions.q: The second parameter of main can also be declared as char **argv instead of char *argv[].
questions.explain: Both forms describe argv as an array of strings (char pointers).
argc is the argument count: the number of command line arguments, including the program name.
argv is the argument vector: an array holding the value of each command line argument.

questions.q:
A user runs: ./a.out 10 11 200
What value does argc hold?
questions.explain: The program name counts as the first argument, plus 10, 11, and 200: 4 in total.

questions.q:
A user runs: ./prog input.txt
What value does argc hold?
questions.explain: argc counts the program name (prog) and input.txt, so it is 2.

questions.q: argc counts only the arguments typed after the program name, not the program name itself.
questions.explain: argc includes the program name. Running ./a.out with no other arguments gives argc = 1.

questions.q:
A user runs: ./a.out 10 11 200
How many elements does the argv array contain, counting the terminating element?
questions.explain: argv has argc + 1 elements: 4 argument strings followed by NULL.

questions.q: What value is stored in the last element of argv (argv[argc]), marking the end of the argument list?
questions.explain: The first argc elements hold the argument strings and the final element is NULL.

questions.q:
A user runs: ./a.out 10 11 200
What is stored in argv[2]?
questions.explain: argv[0] is the program name, argv[1] is "10", argv[2] is "11", and argv[3] is "200". Every argument is passed as a string, not an int.

questions.q: When a user types a number such as 10 on the command line, it arrives in argv as an int.
questions.explain: Every command line argument is passed in as a string, so 10 arrives as "10". The program must convert it to get an integer.

questions.q: Which statements about argv are true?
choices: It is an array of strings (char arrays)
It has exactly argc elements, with no terminator
questions.explain: argv holds argc argument strings, starting with the program name, followed by a final NULL element: argc + 1 elements in total.

questions.q: What does the name atoi stand for?
questions.explain: atoi ("a to i") converts a string of digit characters to the matching integer value.
argv[1] is the string "10", and atoi converts it to the int 10.

questions.q:
A user runs: ./a.out 10 11 200
What does atoi(argv[1]) + atoi(argv[3]) evaluate to?
questions.explain: argv[1] is "10" and argv[3] is "200". Converted, they are 10 + 200 = 210.

questions.q: A program wants to do arithmetic with a number passed on the command line. Why does it need a function like atoi?
choices: Command line arguments arrive as strings and must be converted to an integer type first
argc only stores the first digit of each argument
argv stores numbers in reverse order
Command line arguments can only be read once
questions.explain: Each argument is a string such as "10". C's standard library has functions like atoi to convert strings to other types.
